name: Kinabalu Park
blurb: Cloud forest where tree shrews feed giant pitcher plants.

tip.title: Dry out the cloud forest
tip.text: Set Rainfall to -100% and watch the pitcher plants, oaks and figs first, then the shrews, rats, birds and the pitviper that depend on them.

sources.title: Mongabay: small mammals use Borneo pitcher plant as toilet in exchange for nectar

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Kinabalu Park, Mountain treeshrew, Trimeresurus sabahi). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Light reaches the canopy and the open ridges; cloud often cuts it back on the upper slopes.
Moist air from the sea condenses on the mountain, keeping the montane forest wet and mossy.
Figs bear fruit that many forest birds and mammals eat. A fig species is among the commonly recorded plants near the park.

nodes.name: Fungi, leeches & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood and dead animals in the damp forest floor and return nutrients to the soil.

story: Kinabalu Park in Sabah, Malaysian Borneo surrounds Mount Kinabalu, at 4,095.2 metres the highest mountain on Borneo. Established in 1964, it became Malaysia's first World Heritage Site in December 2000.
matters: It holds more than 4,500 species of plants and animals. UNESCO identifies it as a Centre of Plant Diversity for Southeast Asia, with at least half of Borneo's plant species.
